screens.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRPs)
screens.narratorSegment: In any routed network the default gateway is your hosts' lifeline to other subnets. When that single gateway fails, hosts are isolated even when other network links exist. In this lesson you will learn how First Hop Redundancy Protocols, or FHRPs, solve that single-point-of-failure by presenting a virtual router to hosts and allowing multiple physical devices to share that responsibility. We'll work through the operational principles of HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP, see how priorities and preemption influence election, and practice a common HSRP configuration that uses tracking to prevent a gateway without upstream connectivity from remaining primary. You will also learn how GLBP can actively distribute hosts across multiple routers to utilize redundant gateway capacity. Knowing when to use each protocol matters: use HSRP or VRRP when you want simple active/standby redundancy and GLBP when you need built-in gateway load balancing. By the end you should be able to configure HSRP on two routers, interpret verification output, and design tracking so that the active gateway always has a viable path. Let us begin by exploring the gateway failure problem and the core options for a resilient default gateway.

screens.title: Default gateway as a single point of failure
screens.narratorSegment: Start with the problem: hosts send traffic to a single default gateway IP when reaching other subnets. If the physical device owning that gateway IP fails, every host loses outbound reachability even if redundant Layer 2 connectivity exists. This is the single point of failure we must remove. First Hop Redundancy Protocols solve this by creating a virtual router that multiple routers can share. Hosts keep using the same gateway address, but control of that virtual address moves between devices when failures occur. A concrete example: a VLAN with hundreds of endpoints uses 192.168.10.254 as the gateway. If Router-1 that owns the address goes down, without FHRP those hosts cannot reach the internet. With HSRP or VRRP another router becomes owner of the virtual address and traffic continues. A common misconception is to rely only on redundant switch uplinks; redundant Layer 2 paths do not protect the default gateway itself. Another misconception is thinking equal priorities alone guarantee optimal paths — preemption and priority tuning matter to ensure the preferred router hosts the active role. The takeaway: eliminate the single gateway by presenting a virtual router so hosts keep their configuration and connectivity even when a gateway device fails. How would you simulate this failure in a lab and verify endpoint reachability?

keyIdea.title: Why FHRPs exist
keyIdea.text: They remove single gateway failure by presenting a virtual gateway that can move between devices.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Default gateway failure
Definition & impact
When the device hosting a subnet's default IP goes offline, hosts lose routing to other networks. Redundant uplinks don't protect a failed gateway process.
  • Virtual router lets multiple devices share one gateway address.
  • Failover must be fast and preserve MAC/IP presented to hosts.
  • Without FHRP, manual reconfiguration or static ARP changes are needed after failure.
Analogy
Think of a virtual receptionist that forwards calls: if one person is absent another takes the role with the same phone number.
Example scenario
VLAN 10 uses 192.168.10.254. Router-1 owns that IP. If Router-1 loses power, hosts cannot reach 10.0.0.0/8 networks without FHRP.
Check your understanding
Describe the steps you would take to simulate gateway failure in a lab and how to verify hosts still reach an external IP after failover.
Key Takeaway

Use a virtual router so hosts never depend on a single physical device for default gateway services.

screens.title: HSRP operational flow and state machine
screens.narratorSegment: HSRP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that creates a shared virtual IP and virtual MAC on an HSRP group. One router becomes active and forwards traffic for the virtual IP; another becomes standby and takes over if the active fails. Other routers remain in listen state. Election of the active router relies on priority values and, as a tie-breaker, the highest IP address. Preemption is optional and controlled with the preempt command: when enabled, a higher-priority router that comes online will take over the active role. A practical example: set Router-1 priority to 150 and Router-2 remains at default 100. Router-1 becomes active. If Router-1's priority is later reduced by a tracking event or it fails, Router-2 becomes active. A common mistake is forgetting to enable preemption when you want the preferred router to reclaim the role after recovery — without preemption a recovered higher-priority device will remain standby. HSRP also supports multiple groups on the same interface so you can spread gateway responsibilities across routers and achieve VLAN-level load distribution. Think of HSRP as an active/standby controller with configurable election and reclaim behavior; the key is matching priority and preemption settings to your operational intent.

keyIdea.title: HSRP in brief
keyIdea.text: HSRP elects an active router by priority and IP tie-breaker; standby takes over when the active fails. Preemption controls role reclaiming.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › HSRP operational flow
HSRP states & election
Active forwards virtual IP; standby monitors active; listen waits. Election uses priority then IP address.
1. Routers join an HSRP group number and advertise hello packets.
2. Highest priority becomes active. If equal, highest IP wins.
3. Preemption allows a higher-priority router to reclaim active status when it comes online.
4. Multiple HSRP groups per interface enable load distribution across VLANs.
Common mistake: forgetting preemption when you expect a preferred router to regain control after recovery.
Practical Example
Router-1 priority 150 preempt enabled becomes active; Router-2 priority 100 is standby. If Router-1 fails, Router-2 takes over immediately.
Why priority matters
Priorities ensure deterministic election. Use higher priority on routers with better upstream connectivity or capacity.
Key Takeaway

Set priorities and preemption to match operational expectations so failover and reclamation behave predictably.

Router-2 uses default priority and preemption enabled. In a lab, apply the interface stanza on each device and then run the verification commands shown. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › HSRP Configuration
Router-1 configuration (preferred)
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 1 ip 192.168.10.254
 standby 1 priority 150
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 decrement 60
!
! Verification commands
show standby brief
show standby 1 detail
Note: adapt interface names and IP addresses to your lab. Standby version 2 provides enhancements and should match on both routers.
Router-2 configuration (backup)
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby version 2
 standby 1 ip 192.168.10.254
 standby 1 preempt
!
! Verification commands
show standby brief
show standby 1 detail
After applying these commands, use the verification outputs to confirm which router is active and to inspect virtual MAC and tracking status.
Pro Tip
When tracking an upstream interface, choose a decrement value that ensures the router's effective priority falls below the preferred backup to trigger failover when upstream is lost.

screens.title: HSRP tracking and dynamic priority adjustment
screens.narratorSegment: Failover should reflect real network health, not just interface state. HSRP tracking lets you decrement the router's priority when a monitored object — typically an interface or an IP SLA — fails. This ensures a router whose upstream link is down will not remain active and forward traffic into a black hole. For example, Router-1 has priority 150 and tracks GigabitEthernet0/0 with a decrement of 60. If GigabitEthernet0/0 goes down, Router-1's effective priority becomes 90, allowing Router-2 (priority 100) to preempt and become active. Implement tracking with the standby track command and choose decrement values strategically so the backup's priority becomes higher when the primary loses its upstream path. Common mistakes include tracking an irrelevant interface or forgetting to tune the decrement value, which can either prevent failover or cause excessive flapping. For robust designs, pair interface tracking with IP SLA checks that validate actual upstream reachability. The main benefit is intelligent failover: the gateway presenting the virtual IP is always a device with a working path to the networks your hosts need. HSRP tracking and dynamic priority adjustment means tracking ensures the active gateway has a working upstream path by reducing priority when monitored objects fail.. In practical terms, making failover decisions sensitive to real network health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Tracking ensures the active gateway has a working upstream path by reducing priority when monitored objects fail.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › HSRP Tracking
How tracking works
Tracking watches an object and decrements the HSRP priority if it fails so election reflects operational readiness.
Configure: standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 decrement 60.
Effect: effective priority = configured priority minus decrements from failed tracked objects.
Best practice: track real upstream reachability (IP SLA) where possible.
Concrete example
Router-1 priority 150 tracks upstream interface decrement 60 → if upstream fails, effective priority 90 gives Router-2 priority 100 the active role.
Common mistake
Not tuning decrement values or tracking the wrong interface may prevent the proper failover decision.
Key Takeaway

Use tracking to make the active gateway reflect not only device health but also upstream path health for reliable failover.

screens.title: VRRP — open-standard redundancy
screens.narratorSegment: VRRP is the open-standard equivalent of HSRP, designed for multi-vendor environments. It provides a virtual IP and virtual MAC so one router becomes the master and others act as backups. VRRP uses priorities in the range 0 to 255, with a default of 100, and falls back to the highest IP address as a tie-breaker. One important operational difference is that VRRP enables preemption by default; you can disable it if you require static role assignments. Another subtle difference is the way the virtual MAC is formed: VRRP commonly uses the physical MAC address of the master router as part of the virtual MAC, while HSRP uses a unique virtual MAC pattern. Practically, choose VRRP when your network includes equipment from multiple vendors or when standards-based behavior simplifies support. A common misconception is that VRRP behaves identically to HSRP; while the purpose is the same, defaults and small behavioral differences like preemption default and virtual MAC construction can affect failover and troubleshooting. The takeaway: pick the protocol whose defaults and vendor support best match your environment and adjust priorities and preemption settings to achieve your failover goals.

keyIdea.text: An open-standard FHRP suitable for multi-vendor networks; similar function to HSRP but with different defaults and virtual MAC behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › VRRP
VRRP essentials
Open standard protocol that elects a master router to own a virtual IP and MAC. Defaults differ from HSRP.
Priority range 0–255, default 100.
Preemption enabled by default; can be disabled.
Virtual MAC typically derived from the master's physical MAC in many implementations.
Use cases & pitfalls
Select VRRP for multi-vendor scenarios. Beware default preemption might cause role switching you didn't plan for; explicitly set preemption behavior to match operational needs.
Misconception
Assuming VRRP and HSRP are interchangeable without checking defaults and MAC behavior can lead to unexpected results during failover.

screens.title: HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP compared
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing the three protocols helps you pick the right tool. HSRP is Cisco-proprietary and provides active/standby redundancy with a unique virtual MAC address. VRRP is open-standard and provides similar active/backup behavior but with different defaults such as preemption enabled by default and virtual MAC formation that often references the master's MAC. GLBP, another Cisco-proprietary option, is distinct because it provides true gateway load balancing: a single virtual IP but multiple virtual MAC addresses, with an elected AVG assigning AVFs to forward traffic. For simple redundancy in a single-vendor environment, HSRP is common. For multi-vendor interoperability, VRRP is safer. When you want to actively distribute hosts across multiple routers, GLBP is appropriate. A key misconception is thinking HSRP can load balance across a single group; it cannot unless you deploy multiple groups per interface. GLBP's load balancing modes — round-robin, weighted, or host-dependent — determine how clients are mapped to AVFs and must be chosen based on traffic symmetry and session persistence requirements. The right choice depends on vendor mix, desired failover behavior, and whether you want active-active gateway utilization. HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP compared means use hsrp for cisco active/standby, vrrp for multi-vendor needs, and glbp when you require active load balancing of gateway traffic.. In practical terms, choose the right protocol for your network needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Protocol Comparison
HSRP
Cisco-proprietary. Active/standby with unique virtual MAC. Priority and preemption control election.
VRRP
Open standard. Master/backup model. Preemption enabled by default; virtual MAC differs from HSRP.
GLBP
Cisco-proprietary. Active load balancing with AVG and AVFs, multiple virtual MACs, and flexible balancing algorithms.
When to choose
Pick VRRP for multi-vendor interoperability, HSRP for Cisco-only deployments needing stable defaults, and GLBP when you want to utilize multiple gateways actively.
Common pitfall
Assuming HSRP provides load balancing in a single group. Use GLBP or multiple HSRP groups for distribution.

screens.title: GLBP architecture: AVG and AVF roles
screens.narratorSegment: GLBP extends gateway redundancy by enabling active forwarding on multiple routers for a single virtual IP. An elected Active Virtual Gateway, or AVG, assigns virtual MAC addresses to routers designated as Active Virtual Forwarders, AVFs. The AVG answers ARP requests for the virtual IP with one of the virtual MACs, distributing clients across AVFs. GLBP supports several balancing options: round-robin cycles assignments, weighted distribution accounts for router capacity, and host-dependent maps clients consistently to the same AVF. A concrete operational consequence is that traffic can flow through multiple physical gateways simultaneously, improving aggregate throughput and utilization of redundant devices. GLBP still uses priorities and preemption for AVG election, so the AVG role can move if a higher-priority router comes online. A common mistake is misunderstanding assignment persistence: host-dependent mode preserves client-to-AVF mapping while round-robin does not, which can affect session persistence. The design trade-off is between even distribution and session consistency. If you need both redundancy and balanced forwarding for many clients, GLBP provides a ready-built solution. Roles and flow
AVG manages virtual MAC assignment. AVFs forward client traffic using assigned virtual MACs. AVG answers ARP to distribute clients.
AVG performs virtual MAC allocation and can be elected by priority and preemption.
AVFs actively forward; they are not pure standby.
Load balancing modes affect persistence and distribution behavior.
Example and caution
If you choose round-robin, new ARP requests rotate among AVFs. For session-sensitive applications, consider host-dependent or weighted modes for stability.
Common mistake
Not understanding balancing modes can produce uneven load or break session affinity unexpectedly.

screens.title: Using multiple HSRP groups for VLAN-level distribution
screens.narratorSegment: If GLBP isn't available or desired, HSRP can still contribute to load distribution by using multiple HSRP groups on the same physical interface. Each group has a unique virtual IP and virtual MAC, and you can configure different routers to be active for different groups. For example, on the same pair of routers you might configure HSRP group 1 where Router-1 is active for VLAN 10, and HSRP group 2 where Router-2 is active for VLAN 20. Hosts in each VLAN use the virtual IP assigned to their VLAN's HSRP group and therefore forward to different active routers. This pattern is especially useful when you want deterministic distribution by VLAN without changing client configurations. The trade-off is increased configuration complexity — you must manage multiple groups and ensure priorities and preemption behave as intended. A misconception is expecting per-host distribution from multiple groups; multiple groups distribute per VLAN or per virtual IP, not automatically across individual hosts in a single VLAN. The takeaway: multiple HSRP groups provide a controllable way to spread load across routers when GLBP isn't an option.

Deploy multiple HSRP groups per interface to make Router-1 active for some VLANs and Router-2 active for others.
Group 1: VLAN 10 virtual IP assigned, Router-1 active.

screens.title: Verify HSRP operation and common troubleshooting steps
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is how you prove a configuration works. The two verification commands shown in the chapter are show standby brief and show standby 1 detail. Show standby brief gives a compact view of groups per interface and identifies the active device. Show standby 1 detail provides timers, virtual MAC, configured priority, effective priority after tracking, and tracked objects. When troubleshooting, first verify that both routers are configured with matching HSRP version and virtual IP, then confirm hello and hold timers are compatible. If failover doesn't occur as expected, check whether preemption is enabled on the intended router, compute effective priority with any configured decrement values, and validate upstream reachability because tracking reacts to interface or IP SLA failures. A common misstep is failing to adapt the track command to the correct interface or SLA target; you might see a router remain active despite an upstream outage if tracking isn't watching the right object. Always run the verification commands after making a change and observe the effective priority and state transitions when you simulate a failure. This methodical approach prevents surprises in production networks.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These core concepts are the vocabulary you will use when designing or troubleshooting default gateway redundancy. First Hop Redundancy Protocols present a virtual gateway so hosts keep their configured default IP and avoid downtime when a physical gateway fails. HSRP is Cisco-proprietary and uses an active/standby model with a unique virtual MAC; configure priorities and consider preemption to control role claims. VRRP is the open-standard alternative with similar goals but different defaults, including preemption enabled by default and often different virtual MAC derivation. Understanding these distinctions lets you choose the appropriate protocol depending on vendor mix and default behaviors. Remember to pair protocols with tracking mechanisms so an active gateway without upstream connectivity will yield to a router that does have a working path. Keep these concepts in mind as you design and operate resilient gateway services.

fullNarratorScript:
In any routed network the default gateway is your hosts' lifeline to other subnets. When that single gateway fails, hosts are isolated even when other network links exist. In this lesson you will learn how First Hop Redundancy Protocols, or FHRPs, solve that single-point-of-failure by presenting a virtual router to hosts and allowing multiple physical devices to share that responsibility. We'll work through the operational principles of HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP, see how priorities and preemption influence election, and practice a common HSRP configuration that uses tracking to prevent a gateway without upstream connectivity from remaining primary. You will also learn how GLBP can actively distribute hosts across multiple routers to utilize redundant gateway capacity. Knowing when to use each protocol matters: use HSRP or VRRP when you want simple active/standby redundancy and GLBP when you need built-in gateway load balancing. By the end you should be able to configure HSRP on two routers, interpret verification output, and design tracking so that the active gateway always has a viable path. Let us begin by exploring the gateway failure problem and the core options for a resilient default gateway.

These objectives will guide our work. First, you will explain why First Hop Redundancy Protocols are necessary: we will connect the idea of a single default gateway to the real outage impact on hosts. Second, you will describe how HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP operate, including roles like active, standby, master, AVG, and AVF. Third, you will configure HSRP, using preemption and tracking so the active router has an upstream path. Finally, you will implement tracking mechanisms that decrement a router's priority when a monitored object fails. Each objective is paired with a short skill you can demonstrate: narrating a failover scenario, mapping protocol roles to devices, applying the provided configuration templates, and explaining a tracked failover example. These are practical skills: on exam-style questions and in real network designs you will use them to avoid host isolation and to ensure gateways fail over intelligently. Throughout the lesson we will show configuration snippets and verification commands so you can practice in a lab environment with confidence.

In this second objectives slide we focus on measurable actions. For explanation, you'll articulate the default gateway failure scenario and trace how a virtual router preserves host reachability. For description, you'll map HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP roles to device behaviors and explain differences like VRRP's default preemption and GLBP's multiple virtual MACs. For configuration, you'll show the given HSRP templates on two routers, enable preempt so the preferred router can reclaim the active role, and add the track command to reduce priority when an upstream link fails. For tracking, you'll demonstrate how decrement values change election outcomes and why that prevents a gateway without upstream connectivity from remaining active. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic or check: simulate an interface failure in the lab and confirm with show standby brief, compare priority numbers, and explain the resulting state transitions. These are the concrete lab skills you will demonstrate when assessed.

Start with the problem: hosts send traffic to a single default gateway IP when reaching other subnets. If the physical device owning that gateway IP fails, every host loses outbound reachability even if redundant Layer 2 connectivity exists. This is the single point of failure we must remove. First Hop Redundancy Protocols solve this by creating a virtual router that multiple routers can share. Hosts keep using the same gateway address, but control of that virtual address moves between devices when failures occur. A concrete example: a VLAN with hundreds of endpoints uses 192.168.10.254 as the gateway. If Router-1 that owns the address goes down, without FHRP those hosts cannot reach the internet. With HSRP or VRRP another router becomes owner of the virtual address and traffic continues. A common misconception is to rely only on redundant switch uplinks; redundant Layer 2 paths do not protect the default gateway itself. Another misconception is thinking equal priorities alone guarantee optimal paths — preemption and priority tuning matter to ensure the preferred router hosts the active role. The takeaway: eliminate the single gateway by presenting a virtual router so hosts keep their configuration and connectivity even when a gateway device fails. How would you simulate this failure in a lab and verify endpoint reachability?

HSRP is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that creates a shared virtual IP and virtual MAC on an HSRP group. One router becomes active and forwards traffic for the virtual IP; another becomes standby and takes over if the active fails. Other routers remain in listen state. Election of the active router relies on priority values and, as a tie-breaker, the highest IP address. Preemption is optional and controlled with the preempt command: when enabled, a higher-priority router that comes online will take over the active role. A practical example: set Router-1 priority to 150 and Router-2 remains at default 100. Router-1 becomes active. If Router-1's priority is later reduced by a tracking event or it fails, Router-2 becomes active. A common mistake is forgetting to enable preemption when you want the preferred router to reclaim the role after recovery — without preemption a recovered higher-priority device will remain standby. HSRP also supports multiple groups on the same interface so you can spread gateway responsibilities across routers and achieve VLAN-level load distribution. Think of HSRP as an active/standby controller with configurable election and reclaim behavior; the key is matching priority and preemption settings to your operational intent.

Now we practice configuration. The provided Router-1 and Router-2 templates configure the VLAN 10 SVI with a physical IP and assign HSRP group 1 the virtual IP 192.168.10.254. Router-1 is set to priority 150 with preemption enabled and tracks its upstream GigabitEthernet0/0 interface, decrementing priority by 60 on failure. Router-2 uses default priority and preemption enabled. In a lab, apply the interface stanza on each device and then run the verification commands shown. After configuration, show standby brief confirms which router is active. Show standby 1 detail gives the current priority, virtual MAC, timers, and tracking status. A common misconception is to paste the template without adapting interface names or IP addresses to the lab topology; always verify interface naming and routing reachability first. When you execute the track test by administratively shutting down the upstream interface, observe the effective priority change and the resulting role transition. Practice this sequence until you can explain why the standby preempt behavior and tracking decrement lead to the observed active/standby outcome. HSRP configuration example (Router-1 and Router-2) means use the given interface templates, enable standby preempt, and verify with show standby brief and show standby detail.. In practical terms, apply the template and verify active/standby states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Failover should reflect real network health, not just interface state. HSRP tracking lets you decrement the router's priority when a monitored object — typically an interface or an IP SLA — fails. This ensures a router whose upstream link is down will not remain active and forward traffic into a black hole. For example, Router-1 has priority 150 and tracks GigabitEthernet0/0 with a decrement of 60. If GigabitEthernet0/0 goes down, Router-1's effective priority becomes 90, allowing Router-2 (priority 100) to preempt and become active. Implement tracking with the standby track command and choose decrement values strategically so the backup's priority becomes higher when the primary loses its upstream path. Common mistakes include tracking an irrelevant interface or forgetting to tune the decrement value, which can either prevent failover or cause excessive flapping. For robust designs, pair interface tracking with IP SLA checks that validate actual upstream reachability. The main benefit is intelligent failover: the gateway presenting the virtual IP is always a device with a working path to the networks your hosts need. HSRP tracking and dynamic priority adjustment means tracking ensures the active gateway has a working upstream path by reducing priority when monitored objects fail.. In practical terms, making failover decisions sensitive to real network health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VRRP is the open-standard equivalent of HSRP, designed for multi-vendor environments. It provides a virtual IP and virtual MAC so one router becomes the master and others act as backups. VRRP uses priorities in the range 0 to 255, with a default of 100, and falls back to the highest IP address as a tie-breaker. One important operational difference is that VRRP enables preemption by default; you can disable it if you require static role assignments. Another subtle difference is the way the virtual MAC is formed: VRRP commonly uses the physical MAC address of the master router as part of the virtual MAC, while HSRP uses a unique virtual MAC pattern. Practically, choose VRRP when your network includes equipment from multiple vendors or when standards-based behavior simplifies support. A common misconception is that VRRP behaves identically to HSRP; while the purpose is the same, defaults and small behavioral differences like preemption default and virtual MAC construction can affect failover and troubleshooting. The takeaway: pick the protocol whose defaults and vendor support best match your environment and adjust priorities and preemption settings to achieve your failover goals.

Comparing the three protocols helps you pick the right tool. HSRP is Cisco-proprietary and provides active/standby redundancy with a unique virtual MAC address. VRRP is open-standard and provides similar active/backup behavior but with different defaults such as preemption enabled by default and virtual MAC formation that often references the master's MAC. GLBP, another Cisco-proprietary option, is distinct because it provides true gateway load balancing: a single virtual IP but multiple virtual MAC addresses, with an elected AVG assigning AVFs to forward traffic. For simple redundancy in a single-vendor environment, HSRP is common. For multi-vendor interoperability, VRRP is safer. When you want to actively distribute hosts across multiple routers, GLBP is appropriate. A key misconception is thinking HSRP can load balance across a single group; it cannot unless you deploy multiple groups per interface. GLBP's load balancing modes — round-robin, weighted, or host-dependent — determine how clients are mapped to AVFs and must be chosen based on traffic symmetry and session persistence requirements. The right choice depends on vendor mix, desired failover behavior, and whether you want active-active gateway utilization. HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP compared means use hsrp for cisco active/standby, vrrp for multi-vendor needs, and glbp when you require active load balancing of gateway traffic.. In practical terms, choose the right protocol for your network needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

GLBP extends gateway redundancy by enabling active forwarding on multiple routers for a single virtual IP. An elected Active Virtual Gateway, or AVG, assigns virtual MAC addresses to routers designated as Active Virtual Forwarders, AVFs. The AVG answers ARP requests for the virtual IP with one of the virtual MACs, distributing clients across AVFs. GLBP supports several balancing options: round-robin cycles assignments, weighted distribution accounts for router capacity, and host-dependent maps clients consistently to the same AVF. A concrete operational consequence is that traffic can flow through multiple physical gateways simultaneously, improving aggregate throughput and utilization of redundant devices. GLBP still uses priorities and preemption for AVG election, so the AVG role can move if a higher-priority router comes online. A common mistake is misunderstanding assignment persistence: host-dependent mode preserves client-to-AVF mapping while round-robin does not, which can affect session persistence. The design trade-off is between even distribution and session consistency. If you need both redundancy and balanced forwarding for many clients, GLBP provides a ready-built solution. GLBP architecture: AVG and AVF roles means avg assigns virtual macs to avfs to let multiple routers actively forward for one virtual ip, enabling gateway load balancing.. In practical terms, how glbp enables active-active gateway forwarding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

If GLBP isn't available or desired, HSRP can still contribute to load distribution by using multiple HSRP groups on the same physical interface. Each group has a unique virtual IP and virtual MAC, and you can configure different routers to be active for different groups. For example, on the same pair of routers you might configure HSRP group 1 where Router-1 is active for VLAN 10, and HSRP group 2 where Router-2 is active for VLAN 20. Hosts in each VLAN use the virtual IP assigned to their VLAN's HSRP group and therefore forward to different active routers. This pattern is especially useful when you want deterministic distribution by VLAN without changing client configurations. The trade-off is increased configuration complexity — you must manage multiple groups and ensure priorities and preemption behave as intended. A misconception is expecting per-host distribution from multiple groups; multiple groups distribute per VLAN or per virtual IP, not automatically across individual hosts in a single VLAN. The takeaway: multiple HSRP groups provide a controllable way to spread load across routers when GLBP isn't an option.

Verification is how you prove a configuration works. The two verification commands shown in the chapter are show standby brief and show standby 1 detail. Show standby brief gives a compact view of groups per interface and identifies the active device. Show standby 1 detail provides timers, virtual MAC, configured priority, effective priority after tracking, and tracked objects. When troubleshooting, first verify that both routers are configured with matching HSRP version and virtual IP, then confirm hello and hold timers are compatible. If failover doesn't occur as expected, check whether preemption is enabled on the intended router, compute effective priority with any configured decrement values, and validate upstream reachability because tracking reacts to interface or IP SLA failures. A common misstep is failing to adapt the track command to the correct interface or SLA target; you might see a router remain active despite an upstream outage if tracking isn't watching the right object. Always run the verification commands after making a change and observe the effective priority and state transitions when you simulate a failure. This methodical approach prevents surprises in production networks.

These core concepts are the vocabulary you will use when designing or troubleshooting default gateway redundancy. First Hop Redundancy Protocols present a virtual gateway so hosts keep their configured default IP and avoid downtime when a physical gateway fails. HSRP is Cisco-proprietary and uses an active/standby model with a unique virtual MAC; configure priorities and consider preemption to control role claims. VRRP is the open-standard alternative with similar goals but different defaults, including preemption enabled by default and often different virtual MAC derivation. Understanding these distinctions lets you choose the appropriate protocol depending on vendor mix and default behaviors. Remember to pair protocols with tracking mechanisms so an active gateway without upstream connectivity will yield to a router that does have a working path. Keep these concepts in mind as you design and operate resilient gateway services.

Focus on these role names and mechanisms as you operate FHRPs. The Active Router in HSRP, or the Master in VRRP, is the device currently forwarding traffic for the virtual IP. In GLBP the Active Virtual Gateway, AVG, assigns virtual MAC addresses and the Active Virtual Forwarders, AVFs, do the actual forwarding. Preemption controls whether a higher-priority device reclaims the active role when it becomes available again. FHRP tracking dynamically reduces priority when a monitored object fails so the election process favors routers with working upstream paths. Remembering these roles and mechanisms helps you read verification outputs and design predictable failover behavior. When you combine correct priority settings, preemption choices, and tracking, your default gateway redundancy behaves in an operationally reliable and testable way.
